title: Forty Minutes

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 22: When the plan breaks, go back to the principle.*

"Forty centimeters," Lio said. His voice remained steady, though his hands betrayed the tremor in his fingers, hovering against the cold alloy. "The crack runs the full length of the visible face. The thermal map showed a spot. The eye sees a line."

Kess stared at the screen. The planned sleeve was a perfect, elegant ring of metal, twenty-five centimeters in length, designed to clamp over the specific, predictable failure point. It was a solution that had survived three pressure tests, two council votes, and one very persuasive argument from Pim about how apples needed sun. It was not a solution that covered forty centimeters.

"Window?" she asked.

"Closing in twelve minutes," Voss said from behind her. He was staring at the clock on the wall, his ginger beard twitching with the agitation of a man watching a pressure gauge creep upward. "The wing is moving out of the reactor's shadow. Once it hits direct thermal load, the coolant expands. We do not patch a hot pipe in vacuum, Kess. It will burst."

The hum of the pump house seemed to rise in pitch, a low, anxious thrum that vibrated in Kess's teeth. She looked at Lio, then at the schematic on her tablet, then back to the trembling hands. The silence in the airlock pressed against her eardrums, thick and heavy as the atmosphere outside.

"Abort?" Lio asked. He did not look at her. He looked at the crack, a dark hairline fracture in the bright metal that looked like a mistake in the metal's own grammar. "That is the protocol."

"That is the safe protocol," Kess said. She tapped the screen, zooming in on the joint. The numbers were still there. The margin was still there. Three point one percent. The orchard was still there, waiting in the dark of Drum Three, the leaves curling slightly as the power fluctuated.

"If we abort," she said slowly, "the leak continues. The coolant loss continues. The heat rejection drops another zero point four percent next month. And in six months, we are cutting the lights anyway."

"Six months is a long time," Voss said.

"Six months is a long time," Kess agreed. She looked at Lio. "Do you have the spare?"

Lio’s eyes widened, then narrowed. "The one Daro made? The one he said was a 'just in case' that looked like a mistake?"

"Does it fit?"

"It fits," Lio said. "But it is not the right shape. It is a cylinder, not a ring. And it is heavy."

Kess nodded. She was already thinking about the clamp spacing, about the stress on the overlap, calculating the torque required to hold a shape that defied the geometry of the joint. "Can you move it?"

"I can move it," Lio said. "But the window, Kess. We have ten minutes."

"Then we move it," Kess said. "And we pray that Daro’s 'mistake' is better engineered than his excuses."
pages.image: Kess in green coverall leans over a tablet screen showing a metal joint, while Lio in a navy EVA suit stands near a large pipe, and Voss watches a clock, tense faces in a dim industrial room.

pages.text:
Kess did not pray. She calculated. The spare sleeve was a straight cylinder, twenty-eight centimeters long, slightly wider than the pipe. It was not a ring. It was a tube. To use it, she had to slide it over the crack, centered on the worst part of the fracture, and then clamp it shut. But the clamps were spaced for a ring. If she used the standard spacing, the metal would flex, and the seal would break.

"Voss," she said, her voice sharp. "Bring the clamp table."

He was there before she finished the sentence. He slid the tablet across the desk, his hands rough and quick.

"Standard spacing is every ten centimeters," Kess said, tapping the screen. "If we center the cylinder on the crack, the ends are free. The load will concentrate on the two middle clamps. The gasket will tear."

"Then we add clamps," Voss said.

"We don't have enough clamps."

"We have the spare kit," Voss said. He pulled a small box from his coverall. "Daro packed it with the cylinder. He said, 'For the heavy lifting, and the heavy thinking.'"

Kess looked at the box. Inside were four additional clamp bands, each one a precise, silver ring. She picked one up, feeling its heft in her palm.

"Center the cylinder on the crack," she said. "Use the standard clamps on the overlap, and add the spares on the ends. The seal compression will be uneven, but the redundancy will hold."

Voss frowned. "The stress on the overlap?"

"It is high," Kess admitted. "But the cylinder is thicker. It will take the load. And if it fails, we are no worse off than we are now."

"It is a gamble," Voss said.

"It is engineering," Kess corrected. "With a little bit of luck."

Lio was already moving, his boots clanking on the deck. "I am ready," he said. "Send me the numbers. The torque specs. The clamp order."

Kess typed it out, her fingers flying over the keys. "Torque to eighty newton-meters. Start with the center clamps, then the ends. Tighten in a cross pattern. Do not skip a step."

"I will not skip a step," Lio said. He paused at the airlock door. "Kess?"

"Yeah?"

"Thank you for not letting me abort."

She looked at him, then at the screen. "I would have had to explain to Brandt why we let a crack win. She would have made it very awkward."

Lio almost smiled. He pulled his helmet down, the glass fogging for a second before the fans kicked in. "Forty minutes," he said. "Let us see if Daro knows what he is doing."
pages.image: Kess and Voss huddle over a tablet and a box of metal clamps, Lio in his EVA suit stands by the airlock door, hands on his knees, ready to move. IMAGE: In a dim workshop, Kess and Voss examine a small box of metal rings, while Lio in a white EVA suit stands by a heavy door, looking tense but determined.

pages.text:
The airlock cycled with a hiss that sounded like a sigh. Lio stepped out into the void, his mag-boots locking onto the rail with a sharp *thunk*. The stars were not stars; they were pinpricks of light on a black sheet, cold and distant. The radiator wing glimmered silver in the reactor's shadow, a vast, silent forest of metal.

"Deploying sleeve," Lio said. His voice was calm, but Kess could hear the effort in it. He moved the cylinder into position, his arms straining against the zero-g drag. "Centering on the crack."

"Confirming center," Kess said. "Visual check."

She watched the screen. Lio’s gloved hands were steady. He slid the cylinder over the pipe, the metal sliding with a smooth, silent grace. It sat over the crack, covering the worst of it, but leaving the ends exposed.

"Clamps," Kess said. "Start with the center."

Lio picked up the first clamp. It was a heavy, silver ring. He slid it onto the pipe, then tightened the bolt. *Click.* He picked up the second. *Click.*

"Torque," Voss said.

"Eighty," Lio said. He turned the wrench, his arm moving in a slow, deliberate arc. The gauge on his wrist tablet flashed green. "Done."

He moved to the next clamp. Then the next. The rhythm was hypnotic, a steady beat in the silence of space. *Slide, tighten, check, slide, tighten, check.*

"Two minutes to shadow exit," Pim called from the comms. He was sitting in the chair next to Kess, his glowing-soled sneakers tapping on the floor. "Ten minutes to direct heat."

Lio’s movements slowed. He was working on the end clamps, the spares that Kess had calculated. He tightened the first one, then the second. The cylinder shifted slightly, a microscopic adjustment as the metal settled.

"Stress on the overlap is high," Lio said. He paused, looking at the gauge. "But it is holding."

"Keep going," Kess said. "Do not stop."

Lio tightened the last clamp. He stepped back, his boots unlocking from the rail. He looked at the joint, the silver cylinder gleaming in the dark.

"It is done," he said.

"Wait," Kess said. She was watching the thermal feed. "The seal. The edge of the cylinder."

Lio looked closer. His brow furrowed. "I see a gap."

"How much?"

"A hair," Lio said. "But it is there."

Kess felt a cold prickle on the back of her neck. "Can you close it?"

"I can try," Lio said. "But I am out of clamps."

He reached into his suit, pulling out a small tool, a thin, flexible strip of metal. He pressed it into the gap, using the pressure of his hand to push the gasket tight.

"Pressure test," Kess said. "Now."
pages.image: Lio in a white EVA suit floats in space, tightening a metal clamp on a large silver pipe, his face focused, stars in the background, Kess and Pim watch a screen in a dark room.

pages.text:
Voss opened the bypass valve a quarter-turn, his hand steady on the handle. The mechanism, designed for vacuum, moved with a smooth, silent grace that felt almost disrespectful to the tension in the room. On the pump house wall, the gauge needle began its slow climb, a thin red finger tracing the arc of the dial.

"Two bar," Voss said, his voice flat and pragmatic.

Kess watched the thermal image on her screen. The wing was dark, a vast shadow against the starfield, while the coolant flowed through the pipes, carrying the ship's waste heat out into the void. The crack was covered, the silver cylinder gleaming, and the seal appeared to be holding.

"Four bar," Voss reported.

The numbers ticked up on the display. The ship hummed around them, a low, steady note that Kess felt in her bones, a vibration like a cello string plucked in the next room. She kept her eyes fixed on the edge of the cylinder, on the tiny gap that Lio had pressed shut with his glove.

"Six bar," Voss said.

The gauge climbed further, the needle trembling slightly. The thermal image showed no change, the cold spots remaining cold, the hot spots staying hot. The coolant was contained, the heat was being rejected, and for a moment, the ship felt safe.

"Eight bar," Voss said.

Kess stopped breathing. The gauge hovered at eight, the needle vibrating in place. Then, slowly, with the inevitability of a tide turning, it began to drop.

"Drop," she said, her voice tight. "One point two bar."

Voss frowned, his brow furrowing over his ginger beard. "The seal?"

Kess looked at the screen. At the edge of the cylinder, a tiny, crystalline wisp of white appeared, blooming against the dark metal. It was not a leak, not yet. It was a weep, a thread of coolant escaping the seal and freezing instantly in the vacuum, looking like a smudge of frost on a windowpane.

Lio’s voice came through the comms, sharp and clear. "Weep."

Kess stared at the screen. The wisp was thin, almost invisible, but it was there, a line of white against the silver.

"It is at the edge of the second sleeve," Lio said. "The gasket is not seated."

"Can you fix it?" Kess asked.

"I can try," Lio said. "But I am out of time."

"Eleven minutes," Pim said from his chair, his voice steady despite the tapping of his glowing-soled sneakers. "Ten minutes to direct heat."

Kess looked at the screen, at the wisp, at the gauge, and then at the math in her head. She thought about the orchard, about the trees, about the promise. She thought about the crack, about the seal, about the physics.

"Rotate," she said.

Lio paused. "What?"

"Rotate the sleeve. A quarter-turn. Re-seat the gasket."

Lio looked at the joint. He looked at the gauge. He looked at the stars.

"I can do it," he said. "But it is tight."

"You have eleven minutes," Kess said. "Do it."
pages.image: Lio in an EVA suit floats near a metal pipe, a thin white wisp of ice visible at the edge of a silver cylinder, his face tense, Kess and Voss watch a screen showing a gauge and a white line.

pages.text:
Lio drifted back to the joint, his black mag-boots locking onto the rail with a sharp, reassuring click that echoed in the silent vacuum. He reached out, his gloved fingers finding the cold edge of the silver cylinder, and felt the rigid resistance of the clamps holding the pipe in place. It was heavy, dead weight in the zero-g corridor, and the friction of the metal against its housing made every degree of movement a negotiation.

"Rotating," he said, his voice tight but steady in the comms. "A quarter-turn."

He pushed, and the cylinder groaned, a low metallic shudder that he felt through his palms and up his arms. The metal resisted, then gave way, sliding a millimeter, then a centimeter, the gasket shifting deep within the housing as the seal adjusted itself. He could feel the subtle change in pressure, the way the joint settled into its true alignment, like a graft finally taking hold in the soil.

"Two minutes," Pim said from his chair, his tapping foot the only rhythm in the room.

Lio pushed again, his arms burning with the effort of moving a mass that had no weight but all the stubbornness of the ship itself. The cylinder rotated, the seal seating, the weep stopping. He stepped back, his boots unlocking with a soft hiss, and watched the screen.

"Done," he said. "Check the seal."

Kess watched the thermal image on her screen. The dark void of space remained dark, but the cold spots at the edge of the panel were warming, the bright white wisp of escaping coolant vanishing as the glycol stayed contained. The gauge needle held steady at eight bar, trembling slightly but refusing to drop.

"Seal is tight," Voss said, his gruff voice softer than usual. He looked at Kess, his bushy ginger beard twitching as he wiped grease from his forehead. "It is holding."

Kess let her breath go, slow and steady, and felt the tension in her chest loosen, the cold prickle of dread fading into a quiet, dawning relief. She looked at Lio, who was floating there in his navy jumpsuit, his hands still raised as if ready to push again.

"We are done," she said.

Lio nodded, his eyes tired but bright. He looked at the joint, at the silver cylinder gleaming in the dark, and then at Kess.

"Forty minutes," he said. "Well done."

Kess smiled, a small, exhausted curve of her lips that felt more real than anything she had felt all day. She looked at the screen, at the steady gauge, at the thermal map where the cold was finally giving way to warmth. The ship was safe. The orchard was safe. The future was something they could maintain.

"Bring us home," she said.
